div.p: Peripheral blood circulating glioma cells (CGCs) are crucial for glioma screening, prognostic evaluation, and diagnostic applications. However, reliable methods for efficient CGCs capture and comprehensive clinical evaluation on whether CGCs could faithfully represent complicated heavy equipment (such as MRI) remain insufficiently explored. Here, we present an antibody modification and size screening-based microfluidic (ASM) chip for effectively capturing CGCs, specifically designed for potential clinical translational applications. The ASM chip consists of one inlet, three outlets, one white blood cell clearance area, and one CGC capture area. The performance of the chip was optimized with two typical cell subtypes, namely SU-DHL-4 (to simulate leukocytes) and U251MG-ZsGreen (to simulate CGCs), and the capture rate reached more than 96% at a flow rate of 1.2 mL/h. In real-life applications, CGCs (1-25/mL) were detected in 21 out of 35 glioma patients. We found that the number of CGCs was relatively high in patients with wild-type IDH1 and was positively correlated with Ki67 expression (p = 0.026). The enrichment of CGC was correlated with neutrophils (p = 0.041) and heparin-binding protein (p = 0.0064), suggesting neutrophil-mediated metastasis. Radiomics linked a higher presence of CGCs with larger tumors, severe necrosis, and extensive edema, suggesting a poor prognosis for patients. The ASM chip can effectively capture and quantify CGCs for guiding the diagnosis and predicting the potential prognosis of clinical glioma patients.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Cancer-related death is the second leading cause of human mortality 1 . It is estimated that up to 90% of cancer deaths are caused by metastatic cancer 2 . When tumor cells break away from the primary tumor, enter the peripheral bloodstream, and circulate throughout the body, they are referred to as circulating tumor cells (CTCs) 3 . Upon adapting to the selective pressures of the new microenvironments in various tissues, these cells establish secondary malignant growths, ultimately resulting in cancer-related mortality. Glioma is the most common invasive cancer of the central nervous system (CNS), accounting for 75% of primary intracranial tumors in adults 4 . The median survival time for patients' postdiagnosis is extremely short, typically ranging from 12 to 15 months 5,6 . Traditionally, it is believed that this type of tumor is confined to the CNS because even the incidence of extracranial metastasis of glioblastoma, which is the most malignant, is extremely low (occurring in only 0.4-0.5% of patients), mainly metastasizing to bones, lymph nodes, lungs, and liver [7][8][9] . However, recent studies have indicated that circulating glioma cells (CGCs) are present in the peripheral blood of patients with glioma and display stem cell characteristics 10,11 .

Currently, there are four methods for capturing and detecting CGCs. Firstly, Telomerase activity-based methods described a telomerase activity-based CGCs detection strategy that utilized an adenovirus detection system, which has been shown to successfully detect CGCs in brain tumor patients 12 . Secondly, Müller et al. introduced a cell marker-based method, in which white blood cells from peripheral blood were separated by centrifugation, and then glioma patient peripheral bloodderived CGCs were successfully identified using GFAP staining 13 . Thirdly, Sullivan et al. demonstrated an inertial focusing chip to separate CGCs based on the physical properties of tumor cells, and employed the STEAM staining method to detect CGCs in at least one blood sample from 13 of 33 glioma patients 14 . In another study, a biocompatible polyparaxylene polymer membrane with an 8-micron pore size was used for separation at high flow rates to enrich CGCs without the need for tumor cellspecific capture antibodies, followed by improved STEAM staining, and a CGCs detection rate of nearly 85.7% (36/ 42) was achieved 15 . Furthermore, Gao et. al. invented a method by integrating advanced SE-iFISH with cell molecular detection technology based on tumor cell chromosome aneuploidy. Magnetic beads were first used to capture white blood cells, and then fluorescence in situ hybridization was used to detect chromosome 8 aneuploidy. Among 31 glioma patients, representing all 7 subtypes, CGCs were detected in 24 cases (77%) 11 . Although the above-mentioned CGCs capture and detection methods have achieved encouraging results, the efficient enrichment and capture of CGCs using microfluidic chips still require further improvement.

Herein, we introduce an antibody modification and size screening-based microfluidic (ASM) chip, which can achieve the removal of leukocytes in peripheral blood and the enrichment of CGCs with high purity (Fig. 1a). The ASM chip consists of the leukocyte clearance (LC) area and the CGC capture (CGCC) area. The LC area is modified with anti-human CD45 antibodies to remove peripheral blood leukocytes, and the CGCC area captures CGCs based on their large size and weak deformation ability. We characterized the key parameters of the ASM chip, including injection flow rate and channel design, to achieve higher capture efficiency. SU-DHL-4 (human B lymphoma cells) and U251MG-ZsGreen (glioma cells) were used to optimize the sample injection flow rate and evaluate the chip performance (Fig. 1b). Subsequently, we used the ASM chip to successfully identify CGCs from glioma patients. We then analyzed the relationship between the number of CGCs and the clinical characteristics of patients (Fig. 1c). Finally, we used radiomics to extract the imaging features of glioma patients, and then explored the relationship between the number of CGCs and the imaging features of in situ tumors (Fig. 1d). Overall, the ASM chip expressed great significance for guiding the diagnosis and predicting the prognosis of clinical glioma patients.

div.head: Working principle and optimization of the ASM chip
div.p: The ASM chip, designed based on the principle of antibody modification and size screening, consists of an LC area, a CGCC area, an inlet, and three outlets (Outlet 1, Outlet 2, Outlet 3) (Fig. 2a, SI Fig. 1). The LC area is composed of equilateral triangular columns arranged in a staggered pattern. The width and height of the triangular columns are 100 × 50 μm, the front-to-back distance between the two columns is 80 μm, the side distance is 200 μm, and the diagonal distance is 63 μm. The CGCC area is composed of equilateral triangular columns arranged in a neat and regular pattern, and the size of the columns is consistent with that of the columns in the LC area. The front-to-back distance between the two columns in the CGCC area is 80 μm, but the difference is that in the front half of the CGCC area (f-CGCC), the side distance between the two columns is 15 μm; while in the back half of the CGCC area (b-CGCC) is 10 μm (Fig. 2b).

In the LC area, anti-human CD45 antibodies conjugated with biotin were modified on the triangular columns (for the detailed modification procedure, refer to the Materials and Methods section) to remove leukocytes from the peripheral blood of glioma patients (Fig. 2c), with the goal of initially enriching CGCs that enter the CGCC area. In the CGCC area, the difference in lateral distance between the two columns in the front and back regions can, on the one hand, alleviate the blockage of the chip caused by excessive accumulation of cells on the front side, and on the other hand, considering that CTCs are heterogeneous and have size differences 16 , the ASM chip can effectively capture CGCs of various sizes, including CGC clusters 17 (Fig. 2d).

The working principle of the overall chip is as illustrated in Fig. 2e. Briefly, the peripheral blood of glioma patients is first processed by lysing red blood cells, and then the remained cells are injected from the inlet using a syringe pump, with outlets 2 and 3 blocked with solid steel needles. After a portion of white blood cells are removed in the LC area, they enter the CGCC area. Since CGCs are larger than white blood cells and are not easily deformed, they will be stuck between the two pillars, and white blood cells that have not been completely removed by the LC area will flow out from outlet 1. After the sample injection is completed, the inlet is blocked, and phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) is initially introduced into outlet 1 by a syringe pump to flush the stuck CGCs from outlet 2 or 3 and collect them for subsequent experiments.

To ensure the operational robustness and practical utility of the ASM chip, key hydrodynamic parameters were characterized at an optimized flow rate of 0.6 mL/h. The overall pressure drop from the inlet to the outlet was experimentally measured as 28 kPa, well within the operational range of standard syringe pumps, thereby confirming the chip's ease of use. The flow regime within the device was further analyzed by calculating the Reynolds number (Re) using the hydraulic diameter as the characteristic length. The Re was determined to be approximately 2.6 in the LC zone and below 1.0 in the constricted CGCC zone, both values being far less than 100. These results demonstrated that the flow remains in a stable laminar regime throughout the chip, a condition essential for predictable cell transport, highly reproducible capture efficiency, and the preservation of cell viability through minimized fluid shear stress.

div.head: Optimization of the ASM chip performance
div.p: We optimized the flow rates in the LC and CGCC areas of the ASM chip and evaluated the performance of the ASM chip at various cell concentrations to determine whether the chip can efficiently capture CGCs under complex condition (Fig. 3a). We used SU-DHL-4 cells to simulate leukocytes in human peripheral blood to verify the LC rate of the LC area at different flow rates, ranging from 0.2 to 1.2 mL/h, incremented by 0.2 mL/h. As the flow rate increased, the clearance rate gradually decreased. When the flow rate was 0.2 mL/h, the average clearance rate of the LC area was 98.02% (n = 3) (Fig. 3b). Upon increasing the flow rate to 0.6 mL/h, the average clearance rate decreased to 95.15% (n = 3), the capture of cells in the LC region was shown in SI Fig. 2. Further increasing the flow rate to 1.2 mL/h resulted in a decrease in the average clearance rate to 80.27% (n = 3). Subsequently, we utilized the glioma cell line (U251MG-ZsGreen) to mimic CGCs in order to assess the capture performance of the CGCC area of the chip at varying flow rates. As the flow rate increased, the capture rate of U251MG-ZsGreen gradually decreased, and the capture rate at 0.2 mL/h was more than 99% (n = 3). Even at a flow rate of 1.2 mL/h, the capture rate remained above 96% (n = 3) (Fig. 3c). The results indicated that the ASM chip possesses efficient LC and tumor cell capture capabilities. When combined with the flow rate optimization results from the LC and CGCC areas, which aim to achieve a higher capture rate at increased flow rates, we have decided to adopt 0.6 mL/h as the final sample injection flow rate. Next, we assessed the capture efficiency of the chip across various cell concentrations to mimic the concentration of CTCs in cancer patients at different stages 18 . The concentration of U251MG-ZsGreen cells used in the experiment ranged from 1 × 10 3 to 5 × 10 3 /mL, and the flow rate was 0.6 mL/h. The results indicated that the capture efficiency did not change significantly within different cell concentrations, and the capture rate was above 94% (n = 3) (Fig. 3d), demonstrating that the capture efficiency of the ASM chip remained unaffected by cell concentrations. Since the CGCs captured by the ASM chip can be released from the chip, the cell viability is vital for following cell culturing or further biological research. Therefore, we examined the effects of antibody modification in the LC area and the passage of cells from the CGCC area on cell activity. The CCK8 results showed that there was no difference in cell activity between the three groups at 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h: the LC area unmodified group, the LC area modified group, and the control group without the chip (Fig. 3e). These indicate that our ASM chip can complete the subsequent capture cell identification work.

Considering that the concentration of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) is high and the diameter varies significantly, this might affect the capture efficiency and capture purity of the ASM chip. It was essential to study the performance of the chip with blood spiked with various concentrations of U251MG-ZsGreen cells before capturing CGCs from the blood of glioma patients. We collected approximately 2 mL of peripheral blood from non-glioma subjects, and after red blood cell lysis, obtained PBMCs. The PBMCs were resuspended at a volume of 90 μL of PBS per milliliter of whole blood, and then 10 μL of U251MG-ZsGreen cell suspension at concentrations of 1 × 10³/mL or 5 × 10³/mL were added to prepare simulated samples; the final cell suspension concentration is 4.5-12.1 × 10 7 /mL. Subsequently, the cell mixture was injected into the chip at a flow rate of 0.6 mL/ h (Fig. 3f). The results showed that the capture rate of the CGCC area for tumor cells was always above 94% (n = 3). Further calculations of the capture purity (the proportion of tumor cells in the release fluid out of all cells) and the tumor cell recovery rate (the proportion of the number of released cells to the number of cells captured in the chip) revealed that the capture purity of the chip exceeded 77% (Fig. 3g), and the tumor cell recovery rate was higher than 96% (SI Fig. 3). Bright-field microscopy images revealed the excellent performance of the ASM chip CGCC area in capturing tumor cells (Fig. 3h). Moreover, the LC region effectively removed leukocytes and does not exhibit binding to tumor cells (SI Fig. 4a, b). These results demonstrated that the ASM chip can efficiently capture relatively pure CGCs from peripheral blood.

div.head: An increased number of CGCs is associated with a poor prognosis for patients with glioma
div.p: To verify whether the ASM chip can efficiently capture CGCs in the peripheral blood of glioma patients, we collected blood samples from 35 glioma patients approved by Xinhua Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University, of which CGCs were detected in 21 cases (SI Table 1), and the number of CGCs was between 1 and 25/ mL. In this study, an anti-human GFAP antibody was selected as the identification antibody for CGCs, an antihuman CD45 antibody was used to identify white blood cells, and DAPI was used to identify cell nuclei. CGCs were specifically defined as cells that were DAPI positive, (see figure on previous page) Fig. 3 Optimization of the ASM chip performance. a Schematic diagram of the system optimization for chip flow rate and concentration. For the LC area flow rate optimization, SU-DHL-4 cells were used to simulate leukocytes in human peripheral blood. For the CGCC area flow rate and concentration optimization, U251MG-ZsGreen cells were then adopted to simulate CGCs. b The flow rate used for the optimization of the LC area ranged from 0.2 to 1.2 mL/h. When the flow rate was 0.2 mL/h, the average clearance rate of the LC region was 98.02% (n = 3). When the flow rate was further increased to 1.2 mL/h, the average clearance rate decreased to 80.27% (n = 3). c The flow rate optimization range of the CGCC area was from 0.2 to 1.2 mL/h. The cell concentration was 2 × 10 3 /mL. The rate at 0.2 mL/h was more than 99% (n = 3). Even at a flow rate of 1.2 mL/h, the capture rate was still above 96% (n = 3). d The capture efficiency of the CGCC area did not change significantly between different U251MG-ZsGreen cell concentrations, and the average capture rate was above 96% (n = 3). e CCK8 results showed that there was no statistical difference in cell activity between the three groups, namely the LC area unmodified group, the LC area modified group, and the control group without a chip at 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h. f U251MG-ZsGreen was spiked into the PBMCs of non-glioma subjects to simulate the real condition of CGCs in the peripheral blood of glioma patients. g After U251MG-ZsGreen cells were added to the PBMCs of non-glioma subjects, the tumor capture rate of the CGCC area was still above 95%, and the capture purity of the chip reached more than 77%. h Light microscopy images indicate U251MG-ZsGreen cells captured in the CGCC area. Scale bar: 100 μm GFAP positive, and CD45 negative after immunofluorescence staining. Figure 4a shows the immunofluorescence staining images of CGCs from 4 patients, of note, CGC clusters were detected in patient 4. Subsequently, we compared the differences in GFAP+ cells in the peripheral blood of patients with primary glioma, recurrent glioma, and non-glioma subjects. We found that the number of GFAP+ cells in non-glioma subjects ranged from 0 to 2/mL (SI Table 1), while the postoperative CGC count ranged from 1 to 19/mL in primary glioma patients and from 4 to 21/mL in recurrent glioma patients. There was a significant statistical difference in the number of GFAP+ cells between CGCs from primary and recurrent glioma patients compared to non-glioma subjects. However, no statistical difference was observed in the number of CGCs between primary and recurrent glioma patients (Fig. 4b). This indicated that the number of CGCs in glioma patients was not associated with tumor recurrence. We also compared the difference in the number of CGCs between patients with different pathological grades, and the results showed that the number of CGCs in the peripheral blood of glioma patients with pathological Grades 3 and 4 was higher than that of Grade 2, suggesting that CGC counts correlated with patient prognosis (Fig. 4c). Next, we compared the CGC counts of nine patients using their preoperative and postoperative blood samples. Our findings revealed no significant difference in the number of CGCs before and after surgery (Fig. 4d), suggesting that undergoing surgery did not serve as a determinant for the quantity of CGCs in patients.

Since IDH1 mutation was associated with the prognosis of glioma patients 19,20 , we compared the difference in CGCs between IDH1 wild-type and mutant patients. We found that the number of CGCs in IDH1 wild-type patients was higher than that in mutant patients (Fig. 4e), indicating that a higher number of CGCs might be associated with a poor prognosis in patients. Then, we compared the correlation between the number of CGCs and the expression level of Ki67 and found that the number of CGCs was positively correlated with the expression level of Ki67 (R = 0.4, p = 0.026) (Fig. 4f).

Ki67 is a tumor growth marker. The higher the expression level of Ki67 in tumor tissue, the greater the invasiveness of the tumor and the faster the growth rate, which may be associated with a poor prognosis 21,22 . The number of CGCs is positively correlated with the expression level of Ki67, indicating that vigorous tumor proliferation may produce more CGCs and also suggesting a poor prognosis for the patient. To explore the relationship between CGCs and the peripheral immune environment, we compared the correlation between the number of white blood cells and the number of CGCs, and found that it was positively correlated (R = 0.44, p = 0.045) (Fig. 4g). Therefore, we further explored the correlation between CGCs and neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes. It was found that the number of CGCs was positively correlated with the number of neutrophils (R = 0.45, p = 0.041) (Fig. 4h). However, it was negatively correlated with lymphocytes (R = -0.11, p = 0.62) and monocytes (R = -0.064, p = 0.78), though there was no statistical difference (SI Fig. 5a, b). Related studies have found that glioma patients with postoperative CGC detection have a poor prognosis, and the number of postoperative CGCs was positively correlated with postoperative neutrophil levels 23 , which was consistent with our research results. Finally, we also discussed the relationship between the inflammation-related indicator, heparin-binding protein, and the number of CGCs, and found that there was a strong correlation between the two (R = 0.58, p = 0.0064) (Fig. 4i). The results indicated that a higher number of CGCs correlates with more severe inflammation within the patient's body.

div.head: Patients with detected CGCs have rapid disease progression and poor prognosis
div.p: Considering that CGCs were not detected in 14 of the 35 glioma patients, we followed up the patients and finally obtained the survival and tumor recurrence information of 12 of the 21 CGCs positive patients and 8 of the 14 CGCs negative patients, and explored the differences in their clinically relevant laboratory indicators (Fig. 5a). We found that the death and tumor recurrence rates in CGCs negative patients were 12.5% and 14.3%, while the death and recurrence rates in CGCs positive patients were 41.7% and 42.9% (Fig. 5b, c), indicating that glioma patients with CGCs in peripheral blood have rapid disease progression and poor prognosis. Next, we compared the differences in the pathological grade of the in situ tumors between CGCs positive and negative patients, and found that the pathological grade of the tumors of CGCs positive patients was higher, with the proportion of Grade 3 and Grade 4 reaching 81%; while the pathological grade of the tumors of CGCs negative patients was lower, with the proportion of Grade 2 reaching 78.6% (Fig. 5d); we also found that the Ki67 expression level of the tumors of CGCs positive patients was higher (Fig. 5e). These results indicated that the more aggressive the tumor was, the easier it was to detect CGCs in the peripheral blood. Subsequently, we also compared the differences in the number of cells in the peripheral blood of the two groups of patients, and found that the number of neutrophils (Fig. 5f) and platelets (Fig. 5g) in the peripheral blood of CGCs positive patients was higher than that of CGCs negative patients. A study has shown that the interaction of CTCs with platelets could increase vascular permeability and provide protection against T cells and NK cells-mediated clearance. The interaction of CTCs with neutrophils would increase their proliferation and metastatic potential, promote adhesion and extravasation of The number of CGCs in the peripheral blood of glioma patients with pathological Grade 3 and 4 was higher than that of Grade 2. d There was no difference in the number of CGCs between patients with glioma before and after the operation. e The number of CGCs in IDH1 wild-type (WT) patients was higher than that in mutant patients. f The number of CGCs was positively correlated with the Ki67 expression level. The correlation plots showed the correlation between the number of CGCs and the number of leukocytes (g), the number of neutrophils (h), and the heparin-binding protein (i). *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001 blood vessels, and protect CTCs from immune surveillance 3 . We speculate that CGCs negative patients have relatively fewer neutrophils and platelets, which makes them more susceptible to clearance by T cells and NK cells after entering the blood.

div.head: CGCs abundance could faithfully predict tumor volume, edema severity, and necrosis degree
div.p: We have successfully utilized the ASM chip to capture CGCs in the peripheral blood of patients with early-stage glioma. We speculated that a significant increase in the The mortality rate was low in CGCs negative patients, while it was high in CGCs positive patients. c The tumor recurrence rate was low in CGCs negative patients, while it was high in CGCs positive patients. d The pathological grade of tumors in CGCs positive patients was higher, with the proportion of Grade 3 and Grade 4 reaching 81%; while the pathological grade of tumors in CGCs negative patients was lower, with the proportion of Grade 2 reaching 78.6%. e The Ki67 expression level in tumors of CGCs positive patients was higher than that of CGCs negative patients. f The number of neutrophils in the peripheral blood of CGCs positive patients was higher than that of CGCs negative patients. g The number of platelets in the peripheral blood of CGCs positive patients was higher than that of CGCs negative patients. *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001 number of CGCs post-surgery might be indicative of a poor prognosis for these patients. Consequently, we sought to explore whether this quantitative difference correlated with the imaging characteristics of the in situ tumor. 19 patients with T1-Weighted Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (T1-FLAIR), T2-Weighted Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (T2-FLAIR), and T1-Weighted Contrast-Enhanced Sequence MRI images were included in the subsequent analysis. We initially extracted the imaging features of the tumor and discovered a strong positive correlation between the tumor volume and the number of CGCs (R = 0.61, p = 0.0059), indicating that as the tumor size increased, more tumor cells tended to enter the bloodstream (Fig. 6a). Subsequently, we categorized the patients into groups with large and small tumor volumes based on the median tumor volume, and found that the group with large tumor volumes had a significantly higher number of CGCs (p < 0.05) (Fig. 6b), which further demonstrated that the larger the tumor volume, the greater the number of tumor cells that entered the bloodstream. Next, we compared the correlation between CGCs and other shape features. The results indicated that there was a statistically significant positive correlation between CGCs and parameters such as Surface Area, Maximum 2D Diameter Slice, and Elongation (Fig. 6c). This suggested that tumors with more irregular morphologies, larger diameters, and greater elongation were more likely to cause an increased number of tumor cells to enter the bloodstream. Next, we also explored the relationship between the extracted firstorder features, texture features, and high-level features and the number of CGCs. First, we divided the patients into high and low CGCs groups based on the median number of CGCs. Next, the Wilcoxon test was used to perform a differential analysis of the above features, and it was found that 123 features were upregulated and 29 features were downregulated in the high CGCs group compared with the low CGCs group (Fig. 6d). We extracted the top 5 differential features for analysis and found that the MRI images of the high CGCs group exhibited a high degree of grayscale inhomogeneity, whereas the MRI images of the low CGCs group displayed a significant level of texture roughness (Fig. 6e). The high grayscale inhomogeneity observed in the high CGCs group suggested that the tumor exhibited a high degree of internal heterogeneity, which could facilitate the shedding and metastasis of tumor cells. In contrast, the low CGCs group exhibited higher texture roughness. This pattern implies a heterogeneity dominated by macroscopic structural disorders, such as fibrotic regions, which may physically hinder the effective release of tumor cells into circulation.

Since the severity of edema in patients with glioma was different (SI Fig. 6a), the causes of edema were mostly caused by the damage to the blood-brain barrier of the patients, which caused vasogenic edema 24 . Therefore, we delineated the regions of interest (ROIs) for edema based on the patient's T2-FLAIR sequence, and then extracted the imaging characteristics of the edema to analyze its relationship with the number of CGCs.

We found that the volume of edema was positively correlated with the number of CGCs (R = 0.55, p = 0.014) (Fig. 6f), and the number of CTCs in the large edema group was higher (p < 0.05) (Fig. 6g). This indicated that greater edema would lead to more severe damage to the blood-brain barrier, which in turn would promote the entry of tumor cells into the bloodstream. Finally, we categorized the patients into mild, moderate, and severe necrosis groups based on the extent of tumor necrosis (SI Fig. 6b). The results indicated that the count of CGCs in the moderate and severe necrosis groups was significantly higher than that in the mild necrosis group (Fig. 6h). Previous studies have shown that tumors with high levels of necrosis are typically more invasive 25 , and tumor cells were more likely to break through the basement membrane and vascular walls and enter the blood circulation.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: In this study, we proposed an ASM chip that can efficiently capture CGCs in the peripheral blood of glioma patients. Previous related studies usually adopted either physical properties [26][27][28][29][30] or biological properties to design chips 31,32 . Herein, we employed an integrated effort based on the hybrid design of antibody modification and physical size screening. After optimizing the flow rate and concentration using SU-DHL-4 and U251MG-ZsGreen cells, the average LC rate in the LC area reached 95.15%, and the average capture rate in the CGCC area exceeded 97% at the final infusion flow rate of 0.6 mL/h. Furthermore, the chip's capture performance for CGCs in the blood of cancer patients was assessed using U251MG-ZsGreen spiked blood, achieving a capture efficiency of over 95% and a capture purity exceeding 77%. These results indicated that the ASM chip permitted a high CGCC efficiency and a strong CGC purification capability. After capturing CGCs, we used anti-human GFAP for detection, and the ASM chip managed to imply the presence of CGCs among 21 out of 35 patients. We also compared our method with the existing CGC separation and detection techniques (SI Table 2). The results showed that the ASM chip demonstrated greater stability in separating CGCs and a higher detection rate for highgrade glioma patients compared to many previous studies.

Our clinical investigation with the ASM chip further found that patients with wild-type IDH1 and high Ki67 expression levels exhibited a higher number of CGCs. Both wild-type IDH and high Ki67 expression level indicated that the in situ tumor had vigorous proliferation and strong invasiveness, suggesting a poor prognosis for these patients 20,21 . This suggested that the number of CGCs may be associated with the poor prognosis of patients in a real-life setting. Upon analyzing the relationship between the number of CGCs and the peripheral immune status, we discovered that the number of CGCs was positively correlated with the number of neutrophils. Previous studies have shown that the postoperative CTC status was highly correlated with the overall immunity of the body 23 . The peripheral immune status is characterized by the promotion of inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α, through neutrophil degranulation or enhanced activity. TNF-α is associated with the activation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in inflammatory responses 33,34 . For glioma patients, the levels of CGCs and the expression of NETs-related genes exhibit a notable convergence, which is associated with a diminished cell-killing ability, resulting in immune escape and a poor prognosis 23 . In addition, our results also found that heparin-binding protein was positively correlated with the number of CGCs. Heparin-binding protein is a multifunctional protein secreted by neutrophils, which plays an important role in antibacterial defense, immune regulation, and vascular permeability regulation 35,36 . We hypothesize that neutrophils could be instrumental in tumor metastasis, modulating vascular permeability through the secretion of heparin-binding protein, thereby facilitating tumor metastasis or homing 10 .

Our results indicated that a high count of CGCs might be linked to a poor prognosis in patients. Consequently, we further combined CGCs with radiomics to investigate the potential reasons behind the variation in CGC numbers. We discovered that the number of CGCs was positively correlated with tumor volume, edema volume, and the extent of tumor necrosis. Additionally, we discovered that MRI images from patients in the high CGCs group synchronously exhibited a high degree of grayscale heterogeneity, whereas those from the low CGCs group displayed a high degree of texture roughness. These observations further indicates that a higher number of CGCs post-surgery could potentially suggest a poorer prognosis for the patient. The ASM chip permits a rapid and convenient quantification of CGCs, which offers a complementation or even alternative route, as compared to MRI imaging characteristics, for the diagnosis and prognosis evaluation of glioma.
The ASM chip developed in this study efficiently captured CGCs from the peripheral blood of glioma patients.

CGC counts showed statistically significant correlations with multiple clinical and imaging markers (IDH1 status, Ki67 index, neutrophil count, tumor volume, edema, and necrosis), providing strong proof-of-concept evidence for their clinical relevance. Importantly, the observed detection rate (60%; 21 of 35 patients) reflected the inherent biological characteristics of glioma patients rather than technical limitations. Glioma progression is often confined to the CNS, where the blood-brain barrier restricts CGCs release into the circulation. Moreover, detection rates varied markedly by tumor grade (26.7% for grade 2 and approximately 85% for grades 3 and 4), reflecting the heterogeneity of glioma aggressiveness. These findings indicated that, despite incomplete detection across all cases, the ASM chip remains clinically valuable-its primary role lies in prognostic risk stratification and comprehensive assessment in conjunction with magnetic resonance imaging, rather than serving as a diagnostic tool alone.

This study has several limitations. First, the clinical sample size was relatively limited (35 patients), and this was a single-center study without external validation. This was primarily due to the difficulty in prospectively enrolling a large, homogeneous glioma cohort. Second, we identified CGCs using a stringent triple criterion of GFAP +/CD45-/DAPI+, and demonstrated very low background signal in a non-glioma control group. However, future work will require expanding the sample size and employing more sensitive molecular techniques to thoroughly exclude potential false positives from rare nontumor cells. div.head: Chip fabrication
div.p: The mold consists of a silicon wafer with structures of different heights formed by standard photolithography processes. The SU8-3025 photoresist (MicroChem) was spin-coated on a 3-inch silicon wafer, baked at 65 °C for 2 min, then baked at 95 °C for 8 min, and followed by being exposed to UV light for 140 s through an initial chrome mask with chip design pattern to form 50 μm holes. Then, the silicon wafer was further baked and developed by the developer to attain the pattern on the silicon wafer. The silicon wafer was then baked at 120 °C for 1 h and treated with chlorotrimethylsilane to protect the pattern. Subsequently, the degassed PDMS (mixed with a curing agent in a ratio of 11:1) was poured on the treated silicon wafer, vacuumed for a few minutes, and baked at 85 °C for 45 min. After the PDMS becomes solidified, peel off the PDMS, punch holes for inlets and outlets, and bond the PDMS mold to a glass substrate by oxygen plasma.

div.head: Hydrodynamic parameter calculation and measurement
div.p: The pressure drops across the ASM chip were measured at the inlet using a calibrated microfluidic pressure sensor (Elveflow) during PBS infusion at 0.6 mL/h. The Reynolds number was calculated as:

where ρ ¼ 1000kg=m 3 and μ ¼ 1 10 À3 Pa Á s are the density and dynamic viscosity of PBS, respectively; v is the average flow velocity; and D h is the hydraulic diameter. For a rectangular channel, the hydraulic diameter is defined as:
div.formula: D h ¼ 2wh w þ h
div.p: where w and h denote the channel width and height, respectively. Specifically, in the LC zone, the cross-section measured 80 μm (width) × 50 μm (height), giving D h;LC % 62μm. In the CGCC zone, lateral pillar gaps of 15 μm (f-CGCC) and 10 μm (b-CGCC) with a height of 50 μm yielded D h % 23μm and 17μm, respectively.

div.head: Chip surface modification
div.p: According to previous studies, the chip surface modification process achieves cell capture through antibody functionalization 38 . First, the outlet of the ASM chip was blocked by a solid capillary steel tube, and 4% ethanol solution of 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane (MPTS, Sigma-Aldrich) was injected into the LC area of the ASM chip and incubated at room temperature for 2 h. Subsequently, the chip was thoroughly washed three times with ethanol. Secondly, the LC area was treated with a cross-linker N-γ-maleimidobutyryloxysuccinimide ester (GMBS, Sigma-Aldrich, diluted in ethanol) at a concentration of 10 μM, incubated at room temperature for 1 h, then washed with ethanol and washed three times with PBS (Sigma-Aldrich) to remove excess ethanol. Next, the chip was placed in a humidified chamber, and the LC area was incubated with a 10 μg/mL streptavidin (absin, diluted in PBS) solution at room temperature for 2 h to reduce bubbles formed by evaporation, and then washed three times with PBS. Finally, the LC area was incubated with a 10 μg/mL solution of biotinylated anti-CD45 antibody (BioLegend) diluted in 5% w/w bovine serum albumin (BSA) at 4 °C overnight.

The CGCC area specifically used Anti-Adhesion Rinse Solution (STEMCELL) for pre-treatment. This solution contains anti-adhesion active ingredients, which can form an inert protective film by competitively binding to the hydrophobic sites on the PDMS surface, thereby reducing non-specific adsorption of cell debris or residual white blood cells. First, we used a steel needle to block the inlet, and took an appropriate amount of reagent and injected it from outlet 2 or 3 into the CGCC area. Keep it standing at room temperature for 5 min, then gently rinse with PBS to ensure that the reagent fully covers the surface of the microcolumns.

div.head: Blood sample collection from a clinical sample
div.p: This clinical sample study was conducted in Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, and was approved by the local ethics committee (XHEC-D-2025-040). All blood samples were collected with the patients' consent. Four milliliters of peripheral venous blood were collected from each nonglioma subject. For glioma patients, blood samples were collected once before the operation and again 3 days postoperation, with 4 milliliters of peripheral venous blood each time. Prior to the cell capture experiment, these blood samples were stored in tubes containing EDTA-K2 anticoagulant and were transported and stored at 4 °C.
The cell capture experiment was typically completed within 2 h, and always no later than 24 h.

div.head: Red blood cell lysis
div.p: First, subject the fresh blood to centrifugation at 400-500 × g at 4 °C for 5 min. Carefully remove the supernatant, which is primarily composed of plasma and most of the platelets, to obtain PBMCs. Next, add 6-10 times the volume of red blood cell lysis buffer (Beyotime) to the PBMCs and gently pipette to ensure thorough mixing. Incubate the mixture on a 4 °C oscillator for 10 min to lyse the red blood cells. Then, centrifuge at 400-500 × g at 4 °C for 5 min to discard the red supernatant. After lysis is complete, thoroughly remove any residual lysis fluid and platelets by resuspending the cell pellet in 2-3 ml of PBS and washing. Centrifuge the mixture again at 400-500 × g at 4 °C for 2-3 min and discard the supernatant. If red residue persists, add red blood cell lysis buffer and repeat the above steps until no red precipitate is visible. Finally, resuspend the pellet in PBS solution at a ratio of 100 μl of PBS solution per ml of PBMCs. Then enrich and separate the CGCs within 30 min.

div.head: Microfluidic cell capture
div.p: Before the cell capture experiment, the ASM chip was first washed with PBS to remove excess antibodies and potential bubbles. Subsequently, a flexible Tygon® tubing coated with sodium heparin solution was used to connect the syringe to the chip. Finally, the suspension of red blood cells after lysis was aspirated into a 1 mL syringe. The sample was injected into the chip at a flow rate of 0.6 mL/h for 10 min through a syringe pump (Long-erPump). During the cell capture process, the ASM chip was mounted on a microscope equipped with a highspeed CCD camera (Nikon, Eclipse Ci-S) to observe and record the cell capture process in real time.

div.head: Immunofluorescence staining
div.p: In this study, immunofluorescence staining was used for cell detection and counting. After the ASM chip completed cell capture, the captured CGCs were passed out of outlet 2 or 3 with PBS buffer and collected in a 24-well plate with a glass slide (Corning). The cells were allowed to settle at 4 °C for 1 h. After the cells adhered to the glass slide, they were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) at room temperature for 15 min. Subsequently, the glass slide was washed with PBS, and the cells were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich) solution for 15 min, washed three times with PBS, and finally blocked with 5% BSA for 1 h. Then, the chip was incubated with primary antibodies (anti-CD45 antibody, anti-GFAP antibody) at 4 °C overnight. The next day, the glass slide was washed three times with PBS and incubated with secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature in a light-proof environment. After immunofluorescence staining, the chip was rinsed with PBS, and images were taken using a fluorescence microscope (Zeiss LSM 880).

div.head: Biochemical testing and imaging data collection of glioma patients
div.p: The biochemical test results of all patients included in this study were collected, including blood routine, DIC index, infection index, and thrombosis-related index. At the same time, the patient's MRI data was collected and saved in .dicom format for subsequent radiomics analysis.

div.head: Radiomics analysis
div.p: Radiomics analysis was performed on the collected MRI images of glioma patients. First, the ROIs of the tumor area were manually delineated by experienced clinicians based on T1-FLAIR images using 3DSlicer software (version 5.8.1) (SI Fig. 6c). Next, a total of 1051 radiomics features, including first-order features, shape features, and texture features, were extracted using PyRadiomics software (version 3.1.1) 39 . Texture features were further subdivided into the following categories: (1) gray-level cooccurrence matrix (GLCM), (2) gray-level run-length matrix (GLRLM), (3) gray-level size zone matrix (GLSZM), ( 4) neighborhood gray-level difference matrix (NGTDM), and (5) gray-level dependence matrix (GLDM) features. In addition, a variety of filters were used for feature extraction, including wavelet filters and Laplacian of Gaussian filters. The ROIs of the edema area were extracted based on the T2-FLAIR images, and the feature extraction method was the same as above. The necrotic area was judged by clinicians as mild necrosis, moderate necrosis, and severe necrosis based on the T1-Weighted Contrast-Enhanced Sequence images.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: ImageJ (developed by the National Institutes of Health) was used to analyze fluorescent and bright-field cell images; Auto CAD was used to design the ASM chip; and Origin 2021 was used for data analysis and graphing. Radiomic feature extraction was done using Python (version 3.13.0). All statistical analyses were done using R software (version 4.4.1). The relationships between continuous variables were evaluated by Spearman correlation analysis, and p values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
